title_en: Beijing Xinzhongshi Economic Development Co., Ltd. and Hainan Zhongshi (Group) Co., Ltd. v. China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd. — dispute over real estate project rights and interests
ruling_gist_en: According to the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, if in the first instance the nature of the legal relationship asserted by the parties or the validity of the civil act is inconsistent with the determination made by the court based on the facts of the case, the court shall inform the parties that they may change their claims; if the parties insist on not changing their claims, the court shall dismiss their lawsuit rather than render a judgment on the merits; if the court directly adjudicates on a legal relationship not asserted by the parties, it is both acting on behalf of the parties in exercising their right to sue and depriving the opposing party of its right to defense, constituting a procedural violation.

full_text_en:
Beijing Xinzhongshi Economic Development Co., Ltd. and Hainan Zhongshi (Group) Co., Ltd. v. China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd. — dispute over real estate project rights and interests

Ruling Summary

Pursuant to the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, where during the trial at first instance, the nature of the legal relationship or the validity of a civil act asserted by a party is inconsistent with the determination made by the court based on the facts of the case, the court shall inform the party that it may amend its claims; if the party insists on not amending its claims, the court shall dismiss the action rather than render a judgment on the merits. Where the court makes a judgment on a legal relationship that has not been asserted by the party, it both substitutes for the party in exercising the right to sue and deprives the opposing party of the right to defend, constituting a procedural violation.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2004) Min Yi Zhong Zi No. 107

Appellants (Defendants at First Instance): Beijing Xinzhongshi Economic Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at: East Zone, Third Floor, South Building, Yuexiu Hotel, No. 24 Xuanwumen East Street, Xuanwu District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Wang Tianyi, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Wei, Legal Counsel of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Dang Jijun, Attorney at Beijing Dadu Law Firm.

Appellants (Defendants at First Instance): Hainan Zhongshi (Group) Co., Ltd., domiciled at: 11th Floor, Nanyang Building, Binhai Avenue, Haikou City, Hainan Province.

Legal Representative: Wang Tianyi, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Wei, Legal Counsel of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Dang Jijun, Attorney at Beijing Dadu Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd., domiciled at: 11-14th Floors, Guanhua Building, No. 118 Xizhimennei Street, Xicheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Wang Yin, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Fu Zhaohui, Attorney at Beijing Yihe Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Hu Aijun, Attorney at Beijing Yihe Law Firm.

With respect to the dispute over real estate project rights and interests between the appellants Beijing Xinzhongshi Economic Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinzhongshi Company) and Hainan Zhongshi (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hainan Zhongshi Company) and the appellee China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as China Resources Land Company), the Beijing High People's Court rendered Civil Judgment (2003) Gao Min Chu Zi No. 715 on August 6, 2004. Xinzhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company, dissatisfied with that judgment, appealed to this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held hearings on March 1 and March 4, 2005. The agents ad litem of Xinzhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company, Zhang Wei and Dang Jijun, and the agents ad litem of China Resources Land Company, Fu Zhaohui and Hu Aijun, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

Upon examination, on August 7, 2003, China Resources Land Company filed a complaint with the court at first instance, alleging that: On June 25, 1992, Hainan Zhongshi Enterprise Co., Ltd. (the predecessor of Hainan Zhongshi Company) entered into an agreement with Beijing Xicheng District Huayuan Construction and Development Company (the predecessor of China Resources Land Company, hereinafter referred to as Huayuan Company) to jointly develop a real estate project in the shantytown renovation area on Fuwai Street, Xicheng District, Beijing. The agreement provided that Huayuan Company would be responsible for the preparation of land (three connections and one leveling) and various procedures for project construction, and would receive 20% of the profit from the sale of the housing units; Hainan Zhongshi Company would be responsible for funding arrangements and would receive 80% of the profit. On September 19 of the same year, the parties signed a supplementary agreement further defining the division of work, stipulating that China Resources Land Company's profit share would be increased to 25%. On February 8, 1993, the parties signed a supplementary contract for public construction in the shantytown renovation area, changing the profit-sharing arrangement in the supplementary agreement to a lump-sum fixed amount, with Hainan Zhongshi Company required to pay RMB 50 million and deliver 5,000 square meters of real property. Huayuan Company issued a letter of authorization, fully authorizing Hainan Zhongshi Company to develop the project. On October 20, 1994, Xinzhongshi Company undertook to perform all obligations under the above agreements that were to be performed by Hainan Zhongshi Company. On December 26, 1995, Huayuan Company and Xinzhongshi Company signed a supplementary agreement on the distribution of dividends and profits, changing the original obligation to deliver 5,000 square meters of housing to a cash payment. After Xinzhongshi Company made payments of RMB 10 million in profit and RMB 2 million in interest for overdue payment on August 9, 1996 and January 27, 1997 respectively, it made no further payments. Therefore, China Resources Land Company requested that Xinzhongshi Company pay project transfer fees of RMB 90 million, liquidated damages of RMB 45.79 million (calculated up to July 9, 2003), and bear the litigation costs.

Xinzhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company argued in defense that China Resources Land Company's claims for payment of RMB 90 million in project transfer fees and liquidated damages lacked factual and legal basis, should not be protected or supported, and requested that China Resources Land Company's claims be dismissed in accordance with the law.

The court at first instance found the following facts upon trial: In May 1992, the Xicheng District Planning and Economic Commission and the Xicheng District Urban Construction Management Committee approved the feasibility study report submitted by Huayuan Company for the shantytown renovation on Fuwai Street, agreeing that Huayuan Company would renovate the dilapidated and dangerous houses on Fuwai Street. The total land area was approximately 8.3 hectares, including approximately 6 hectares of land to be requisitioned on behalf of the state and approximately 2.3 hectares of planned land. The shantytown renovation was to be carried out in accordance with the overall urban construction plan of Beijing, focusing on commercial offices and related supporting facilities. The area of dilapidated and dangerous buildings to be demolished was 52,042 square meters, and the area of new buildings to be constructed was 150,000 square meters. The total investment was RMB 708.38 million, including RMB 335.6 million for demolition costs and RMB 372.78 million for construction costs. Construction funds were to be raised through housing reform and real estate development, ensuring a balance of funds with a surplus. Huayuan Company was required to carry out preliminary preparations such as land allocation, demolition, planning, and design with the relevant departments. In the same month, Huayuan Company obtained a Notice of Planning and Design Conditions from the Beijing Urban Planning Administration Bureau, approving the shantytown renovation on Fuwai Street, Xicheng District, Beijing (with the building area to be determined).

On June 25, 1992, Huayuan Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company entered into an agreement to jointly develop the shantytown renovation project on Fuwai Street, Xicheng District, Beijing. The agreement stipulated that the jointly developed above-ground area would be 47,900 square meters, the underground area would be 10,000 square meters, and the land area would be approximately 20,000 square meters (including the municipal apportionment portion). The total investment was RMB 303.09 million, with a unit cost of RMB 5,229 per square meter, including RMB 175.58 million in total investment before the three connections and one leveling, an estimated RMB 115.91 million in project construction investment, and RMB 11.6 million in fees for four sources (water, electricity, gas, heat) and electricity surcharges. The estimated total recovery from external sales was RMB 464 million (unit price of RMB 8,000 per square meter), with a total profit of RMB 160.91 million. Huayuan Company was responsible for handling all procedures before the three connections and one leveling and for demolition and resettlement work, such as project establishment, land allocation, and demolition; for handling various procedures during the construction period; for assisting Hainan Zhongshi Company in organizing design, construction supervision, and final acceptance inspection; and for providing preliminary work plans, demolition schedules, and fund usage plans. Hainan Zhongshi Company was to arrange funds according to the plans, make timely payments of various types, and pay Huayuan Company 20% of the profit from housing sales (after deducting preliminary expenses) in a lump sum. Hainan Zhongshi Company would receive 80%, including the 20% profit to be received by Hong Kong Datong Co., Ltd., which assisted in organizing funds and sales. The parties would form a joint office, operating externally under Huayuan Company's name to develop and organize funds, and internally as a business department of Huayuan Company. In September of the same year, Huayuan Company obtained a Construction Land Planning Permit from the Beijing Urban Planning Administration Bureau, confirming that the land area for the Fuwai Street shantytown renovation project was approximately 7.3 hectares.

On September 19, 1992, Huayuan Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company signed a supplementary agreement providing that Hainan Zhongshi Company would organize all funds, and the parties would share profits with Huayuan Company receiving 25% and Hainan Zhongshi Company receiving 75%. A headquarters was to be formed, with Huayuan Company responsible for project establishment, planning approvals, registration, handling of land use approvals, construction permits, and other procedures, and for organizing demolition. Hainan Zhongshi Company was responsible for funding, design, construction, decoration, etc. The parties would establish a joint venture company. After the signing of this agreement, Huayuan Company was to provide Hainan Zhongshi Company with copies of all official, legal, and valid approval documents, including the red line map approval and land certificate. After Hainan Zhongshi Company paid the first demolition fee of RMB 40 million, Huayuan Company was to provide a mortgage using the purchase contract for the buildings bought with that money or the land certificate. After the joint venture company was established, Hainan Zhongshi Company would transfer these to the joint venture company, and Huayuan Company would provide the original copies of all approvals to Hainan Zhongshi Company, which would later transfer them to the joint venture company. An amount of RMB 11.8 million in preliminary expenses paid by Hainan Zhongshi Company during the preliminary work was to be deducted from the relocation costs. The project was divided into three phases: Phase I, covering 60,000 square meters, was named "Fuhaus Apartment"; Phase II was to the east of this apartment; Phase III was to the west. Where this supplementary agreement conflicted with the June 25, 1992 agreement, the supplementary agreement would prevail. Hainan Zhongshi Company paid a deposit of RMB 500,000, etc. In December of the same year, the Beijing Urban Planning Administration Bureau issued a Notice of Approval of Design Plan, determining that the shantytown renovation area covered 7.3 hectares, including 4.17 hectares of planned land, and the planned building use was commercial office and office buildings.

On February 8, 1993, Huayuan Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company signed a supplementary contract for public construction in the shantytown renovation area, stipulating the following regarding the joint development: The total land area for the joint development project was approximately 8.3 hectares, including approximately 6 hectares of land to be requisitioned on behalf of the state and approximately 2.3 hectares of planned land. The total planned area approved was approximately 200,000 square meters (including underground). The project was required to be built into a modern regional-level comprehensive business facility, large-scale public building support facilities, commercial and residential buildings, apartments, and urban arterial roads, and was to be equipped with seven major municipal pipelines. Cooperation method: (1) Capital investment: All project investment was to be raised by Hainan Zhongshi Company. (2) Profit sharing: The profit-sharing arrangement of 25% and 75% in the September 19, 1992 agreement was modified to a lump-sum fixed profit for Huayuan Company. Subject to Huayuan Company ensuring the area shown on the approved planning drawings, Hainan Zhongshi Company was to pay Huayuan Company RMB 50 million and deliver 5,000 square meters of commercial and office space within the project, with all remaining profits belonging to Hainan Zhongshi Company. In addition to providing the approved planning scheme and various approvals for the project and handling procedures, Huayuan Company authorized Hainan Zhongshi Company to fully develop the project and sell it externally. Hainan Zhongshi Company was responsible for all preliminary work after approval of the project's planning scheme, demolition, resettlement, and leveling within the project's red line, as well as project construction and commercial housing sales operations. Under the above cooperation conditions, Huayuan Company agreed that Hainan Zhongshi Company would carry out the specific operation and implementation of the project. After the start of Phase I construction, Hainan Zhongshi Company would pay Huayuan Company RMB 25 million from 60% to 80% of the sales; after the completion of Phase II, it would pay another RMB 25 million. After the completion of Phase I, 5,000 square meters of usable floor space would be delivered as profit. The payment of land use rights transfer fees and land use fees would be borne by Hainan Zhongshi Company with the assistance of Huayuan Company. Where the September 19, 1992 cooperation contract conflicted with this agreement, this agreement would prevail.

In February 1993, the Beijing Economic System Reform Office approved the establishment of Beijing Huayuan Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huayuan Real Estate Company), with a total capital of RMB 250 million, including RMB 225 million in legal person shares, of which Huayuan Company held RMB 87.03 million in state-owned legal person shares. In June 1993, Huayuan Company was deregistered. In December 2001, Huayuan Real Estate Company changed its name to China Resources Land Company.

On September 23, 1993, the Beijing Urban Planning Administration Bureau replied to Xinzhongshi Company, agreeing that Xinzhongshi Company could commence construction in advance and proceed with earthwork according to the design plan. On October 20, 1993, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company jointly submitted an application to the Xicheng District Planning and Economic Commission to change the name of the project establishment. The application stated that the shantytown renovation project jointly undertaken by both parties had begun relocation, procedures for compensated transfer of land use were underway, and external sales were being fully carried out. To facilitate Xinzhongshi Company's handling of procedures for external and internal sales and relocation, permission was requested to handle the name change procedures for the project establishment with the planning commission under the name of Xinzhongshi Company, without changing the original cooperation conditions and profit-sharing between Xinzhongshi Company and Huayuan Real Estate Company. On November 6, 1993, the Xicheng District Planning and Economic Commission and the Xicheng District Construction Management Committee approved the application of Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company, agreeing to change the project establishment entity to Xinzhongshi Company, with the shantytown renovation task still to be jointly undertaken by the two entities according to the original plan and renovation requirements. On November 11, 1993, the Beijing Urban Planning Administration Bureau issued a notice approving the change of use of the 7.3 hectares of land originally approved for Huayuan Company under (92) Jian Di Zi No. 136 (i.e., the Construction Land Planning Permit) to Xinzhongshi Company. On November 27, 1993, Xinzhongshi Company obtained the state-owned land use rights certificate for the land on the north side of the current road on Fuchengmen Street, Xicheng District, Beijing.

On October 20, 1994, Xinzhongshi Company sent a letter to Huayuan Real Estate Company stating that Xinzhongshi Company was a wholly-owned subsidiary of Hainan Zhongshi Company, and the cooperative development agreement signed between Hainan Zhongshi Company and Huayuan Company would be performed by Xinzhongshi Company on behalf of Hainan Zhongshi Company.

On November 7, 1994, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company signed Supplementary Agreement No. 137, stipulating that the RMB 50 million that Hainan Zhongshi Company was obligated to pay Huayuan Company by the end of 1994 under the contract dated February 8, 1993, would instead be treated as a shareholder loan from Hainan Zhongshi Company to Huayuan Real Estate Company, with interest at a monthly rate of 12 per thousand from December 31, 1994. On the same day, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company signed an internal agreement regarding Supplementary Agreement No. 137, stating that Supplementary Agreement No. 137 was entered into solely to meet the external financing needs of Huayuan Real Estate Company and had no legal binding effect on Hainan Zhongshi Company. During the trial, China Resources Land Company indicated that it did not recognize this internal supplementary agreement.

On December 26, 1995, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company signed Supplementary Agreement No. 184 on the Distribution of Dividends and Profits, stipulating that sales work had been carried out for more than 60% of the area of the first-phase buildings on Fuwai Street, and the profit of RMB 25 million due to Huayuan Real Estate Company would be actually paid to Huayuan Real Estate Company by December 31, 1995. At the same time, Huayuan Real Estate Company would lend the RMB 25 million to Xinzhongshi Company as working capital for a term of six months, to be repaid by June 30, 1996, with a separate loan agreement to be signed. The original obligation to deliver 5,000 square meters of housing was changed to a cash payment to Huayuan Real Estate Company by December 31, 1995, at RMB 10,000 per square meter, totaling RMB 50 million. This RMB 50 million would be treated as a loan to Xinzhongshi Company for a term of 11 months, to be repaid by November 30, 1996, with a separate loan agreement to be signed. The payment of RMB 25 million due after the completion of Phase II would still be executed according to the original agreement. On the same day, Xinzhongshi Company and Huayuan Real Estate Company signed two loan agreements based on the above content, stipulating that the loan of RMB 25 million to Xinzhongshi Company would be repaid with interest in a single installment by July 31, 1996 (a 7-month loan period); the loan of RMB 50 million would be repaid with interest in a single installment by December 30, 1996 (a 12-month loan period), with a monthly interest rate of 12.06 per thousand. Compound interest would be charged on overdue amounts, and a penalty of 10% per month would be added to the principal.

On December 20, 1996, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company signed a Second Supplementary Agreement on the Distribution of Profits from the Shantytown Renovation Project, stipulating that Xinzhongshi Company agreed to pay the profits due to Huayuan Real Estate Company in advance. After Xinzhongshi Company paid the profits to Huayuan Real Estate Company, Huayuan Real Estate Company agreed to waive all project rights and interests. The parties negotiated to modify the terms of the June 25 agreement, the February 8 agreement, and the December 26 agreement: The provision in the original agreement that the profit of RMB 25 million payable to Huayuan Company after the completion of Phase II would still be executed according to the original agreement was changed to an advance payment of the RMB 25 million profit to Huayuan Real Estate Company by December 31, 1996. Except for the modifications in this agreement, other terms of the original agreements remained unchanged. After Xinzhongshi Company fully paid the profits, Huayuan Real Estate Company would waive all rights and interests in the project under the original agreements (except for the loans provided), but would still be obligated to assist in completing the unfinished matters of the project. On December 20 and December 28, 1996, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company respectively signed loan agreements stipulating that Xinzhongshi Company borrowed RMB 25 million and RMB 65 million from Huayuan Real Estate Company, with principal and interest to be repaid by December 28, 1997 and June 30, 1997, respectively.

On March 13, 1997, Xinzhongshi Company issued a confirmation to Huayuan Real Estate Company, the main content of which was: Pursuant to the contract signed in December 1995, Xinzhongshi Company should have paid interest of RMB 7.77 million to Huayuan Real Estate Company in January 1997. Due to financial difficulties, it could not pay the full amount on time. It paid RMB 2 million in January 1997, with an outstanding balance of RMB 5.77 million. Xinzhongshi Company undertook to pay the above outstanding amount by June 30, 1997.

On March 20, 2001, Huayuan Real Estate Company and Xinzhongshi Company entered into an agreement on the amounts payable and interest for the Fuwai project, stipulating that Xinzhongshi Company would pay RMB 500,000 by March 30, 2001; prior to the conclusion of litigation between Xinzhongshi Company and the Bank of China Beijing Branch and the China Construction Bank Xisi Branch, Huayuan Real Estate Company would not demand repayment from Xinzhongshi Company; upon completion of Phase II of the project, all remaining amounts would be paid; Xinzhongshi Company agreed to mortgage the 10,000 square meters of office space in the Guobin Hotel to Huayuan Real Estate Company.

Pursuant to the above cooperation agreements and supplementary agreements, and based on the joint application of both parties, Xinzhongshi Company successively obtained the land use rights certificate and construction permits for the project, changed the project establishment entity to Xinzhongshi Company, and proceeded with the development and construction of the shantytown renovation project. Phase I, including road renovation and apartments and a hotel, commenced construction in 1994. That part of the project is now substantially completed. Xinzhongshi Company stated that due to the large capital investment in the project and the fact that the entire project has not yet been completed, loan repayments to the bank are still ongoing, and a settlement of the project has not been made, so no profit has been realized. Phase II construction has not yet begun. During this period, at the urging of Huayuan Real Estate Company, Xinzhongshi Company made total payments of RMB 10 million to Huayuan Real Estate Company in 1996 and 1997. Xinzhongshi Company did not pay the other amounts due (loans) as agreed between the parties to Huayuan Real Estate Company.

During the trial at first instance, China Resources Land Company admitted that, after obtaining the project establishment approval and planning land use permit in 1993, it did not invest in the project or handle the land acquisition procedures for the construction land, nor did it obtain a land use rights certificate. Regarding the matters agreed between the parties, such as the establishment of a project company and the mortgage of property, the parties did not implement or handle them.

During the first instance, the court of first instance notified Hainan Zhongshi Company to participate in the proceedings. Hainan Zhongshi Company stated that it had not actually performed any of the series of agreements initially signed with Huayuan Company concerning the dangerous building renovation project at Fu Outer Street, Xicheng District, Beijing, and that all rights and obligations under the contracts had been transferred to its wholly-owned subsidiary, New Zhongshi Company, for performance. Hainan Zhongshi Company acknowledged and consented to New Zhongshi Company replacing its position as the contract party and assuming the corresponding rights and obligations. China Resources Company and New Zhongshi Company both expressed agreement to this.

The court of first instance also found that the predecessor of China Resources Company was Huayuan Company. New Zhongshi Company is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Hainan Zhongshi Company, responsible for the development and construction of the Beijing project. Hainan Zhongshi Enterprise Co., Ltd. changed its name to Hainan Zhongshi Company in December 1997.

The court of first instance found upon trial that: The development, operation, and transfer of real estate must be conducted in accordance with the law. China Resources Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company entered into a cooperative development agreement and a supplementary agreement in June and September 1992 for the cooperative development of the dangerous building renovation project. The main contents of both agreements were that China Resources Company would be responsible for project establishment and providing the corresponding construction land procedures, while Hainan Zhongshi Company would be responsible for construction funds and construction work, with both parties distributing profits in accordance with the agreed proportion. The agreements reflected the true intent of both parties and did not violate the law. Accordingly, the two agreements above could be confirmed as having the nature of cooperative real estate project development and were valid contracts. On this basis, the parties signed a supplementary agreement on February 8, 1993, which modified the portion of the profit distribution of China Resources Company under the agreement signed in September 1992, changing it to a fixed lump-sum profit distribution for China Resources Company, but the cooperative development nature between the parties remained unchanged. This agreement signed by the parties was still based on cooperative development and had a cooperative nature. The parties expressly stated in the documents submitted to the government for project establishment approval that the original cooperative conditions and profit distribution would not be changed, and permission was sought to handle the project establishment name change procedures in the name of New Zhongshi Company. While approving the change of the project establishment entity to New Zhongshi Company, the government required that the dangerous building renovation tasks still be undertaken cooperatively by China Resources Company and New Zhongshi Company. Therefore, it should be confirmed that, on the premise of not changing the cooperative relationship, the parties agreed to transfer the project to New Zhongshi Company for development and construction. New Zhongshi Company thus obtained the development and construction procedures for the project, became the project owner, and actually carried out the construction. Based on the above findings of fact and evidence, New Zhongshi Company's acquisition of the development and construction rights for the dangerous building renovation project was entirely based on the cooperative relationship between the parties, not a transfer of project rights from China Resources Company. China Resources Company's assertion of a project transfer lacked basis and was not confirmed.

On February 8, 1993, the parties signed a supplementary agreement stipulating that the profit distribution of China Resources Company in the cooperative project would be fixed in a lump sum to be paid by Hainan Zhongshi Company to China Resources Company. This should be regarded as China Resources Company's transfer of its own rights and interests that should be obtained from the cooperative project. New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company repeatedly, through various forms, confirmed by making payments to China Resources Company and promised to pay the amounts that China Resources Company should receive, but to date have not fully honored the payments to China Resources Company, violating the principle of good faith. Therefore, China Resources Company's claim for New Zhongshi Company to pay a transfer price of RMB 90 million was supported. Because Hainan Zhongshi Company was the contracting party of the cooperative agreements and supplementary agreements between the parties, its transfer of the contract rights and obligations to be enjoyed and performed by its wholly-owned subsidiary New Zhongshi Company was an internal corporate act, and China Resources Company had no objection. Although the project was now obtained by New Zhongshi Company, Hainan Zhongshi Company's contractual liability could not be exempted. Therefore, Hainan Zhongshi Company and New Zhongshi Company should jointly bear the payment obligation to China Resources Company.

Considering that the parties' cooperative development and operation of the real estate project were not sufficiently standardized, and given that the form and conditions of the benefits obtained by China Resources Company were changed multiple times, both parties bore some responsibility for causing the current dispute. Based on the actual circumstances of this case, the failure of New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company to pay should not be treated as a breach of contract. China Resources Company's request for payment of liquidated damages was not supported. In summary, in accordance with Article 88, Paragraph 1 and Article 106, Paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment was: (1) New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company shall pay RMB 90 million to China Resources Company within thirty days after the judgment takes effect; (2) China Resources Company's other claims were dismissed. The case acceptance fee was RMB 688,960, of which China Resources Company was to bear RMB 238,960, and New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company were to bear RMB 450,000.

New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this court, requesting that the first-instance judgment be set aside, all of China Resources Company's claims be dismissed, and litigation costs be borne by China Resources Company. Main reasons: 1. China Resources Company asserted that the relationship between the parties was a project transfer. The court of first instance found based on the facts that there was no project transfer relationship but rather a cooperative development relationship. When China Resources Company, after clarification, insisted on not changing its claims, the court should have dismissed its claims. Without trying the cooperative development issue, the court of first instance arbitrarily changed the project transfer dispute to a cooperative development dispute and directly adjudicated that New Zhongshi Company bear the payment liability, which constituted adjudicating on a matter not sued upon, violating the basic principle of "no trial without complaint" in the Civil Procedure Law and depriving New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company of their right to defend. 2. Hainan Zhongshi Company did not actually perform the contract, and China Resources Company did not assert any rights against Hainan Zhongshi Company. New Zhongshi Company's replacement of Hainan Zhongshi Company constituted a change of contract parties. Therefore, Hainan Zhongshi Company should not have been listed as the original defendant nor should it bear joint payment liability. 3. The evidence provided by China Resources Company regarding its predecessor being Huayuan Company could not prove its legitimate plaintiff status at first instance. 4. The statute of limitations for this case had expired. 5. China Resources Company's conduct constituted illegal resale of approval documents. The supplementary agreement of February 28, 1993, violated the mandatory provisions of the State Council's administrative regulations prohibiting real estate companies from reselling or transferring commercial housing construction plans and should be deemed invalid. The so-called project transfer price also constituted illegal profits and should not be supported.

China Resources Company argued in response that the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly and should be affirmed. Main reasons: 1. The basis for China Resources Company's lawsuit was the legal fact that the parties voluntarily signed several agreements, not a legal relationship of project transfer. The court of first instance conducted the trial around the basis of China Resources Company's lawsuit. Both parties fully presented evidence, cross-examined, and debated in court. There was no circumstance of depriving New Zhongshi Company of its right to defend. 2. The cause of action determined by China Resources Company at the time of filing the lawsuit was a dispute over real estate project transfer. Through examination of the evidence, the court of first instance further refined the cause of action to a dispute over real estate project rights and interests (transfer), which was not improper. When concluding a case, a court has the authority and should determine the cause of action based on the actual legal relationship existing between the parties as found by the court. 3. The court of first instance, ex officio, added Hainan Zhongshi Company as the original defendant and informed the parties. New Zhongshi Company expressly acknowledged this in court. 4. China Resources Company not only submitted corresponding evidence regarding its subject status, but the several successive agreements signed by the parties also indicated that New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company acknowledged the name change and subject identity of China Resources Company. 5. The parties had been negotiating regarding the amount and payment of the transfer price, and the creditor's rights in this case had not exceeded the statute of limitations. 6. The nature of the agreements in this case was cooperative development of a real estate project, representing the true intent of both parties on the basis of equality and voluntariness, and did not violate the legal provisions in force at the time; they were valid agreements. China Resources Company had performed its obligations as agreed. The investment in the project and payment of land transfer fees were New Zhongshi Company's contractual obligations. 7. The two regulations cited by New Zhongshi Company regarding "illegal resale of approval documents" could not be applied to this case because they could not be used to adjust civil juristic acts and were not laws or administrative regulations.

The court of second instance found upon trial that: After the conclusion of the first-instance trial, the court of first instance, having found that the "real estate project transfer relationship" asserted by China Resources Company did not exist, exercised its right of clarification and informed China Resources Company to change its claims. China Resources Company insisted on not changing them.

The other facts found by the court of second instance were essentially the same as those found by the court of first instance.

Opinion of the Court: During the first instance, China Resources Company, in its statement of claim, court submissions, and attached evidentiary materials, clearly stated that the basis for its claim for the project transfer price was the existence of a real estate project transfer legal relationship between the parties. The court of first instance, based on the facts found upon trial, believed that the "project transfer relationship" asserted by China Resources Company could not be established. Therefore, after the conclusion of the trial and before the first-instance judgment, it repeatedly exercised its right of clarification, informing China Resources Company to change its claims, otherwise it would bear the litigation risk itself. However, China Resources Company refused to change its claims.

According to the provisions of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Procedures, if, during the first-instance proceedings, the nature of the legal relationship or the validity of a civil act asserted by a party is inconsistent with the determination made by the court of first instance based on the facts of the case, the court of first instance shall inform the party that it may change its claims. In this case, after being informed by the court of first instance, China Resources Company still did not change its claims. Since the nature of the legal relationship asserted by China Resources Company was inconsistent with the determination made by the court of first instance based on the facts of the case, the court of first instance should not have rendered a substantive judgment but should have dismissed China Resources Company's lawsuit. Under the circumstance where China Resources Company still did not change its claims after clarification, the court of first instance directly adjudicated on a legal relationship not asserted by China Resources Company, which both usurped China Resources Company's right to sue and deprived New Zhongshi Company and Hainan Zhongshi Company of their right to defend, violating the statutory procedure for civil case trial by the people's courts.

In summary, the first-instance judgment violated statutory procedure and should be corrected. In accordance with Article 108, Paragraph 1, Item (1) and Item (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 186 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 35 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Procedures, the ruling is as follows:

1. The civil judgment (No. 715, [2003], High Civil First Instance) of the Beijing High People's Court is set aside;

2. The lawsuit filed by China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd. is dismissed.

The case acceptance fee for each of the first instance and second instance is RMB 50, to be borne by China Resources Land (Beijing) Co., Ltd.

This ruling is final.
